question: I handle a trust that has some unique soil; some of it is gumbo, and some is better black and sand. Most are under pivot. I need some help with how to deal with this to improve the soil and be able to keep it under pivot. We had it tiled a few years ago, but it did not work, and we're unsure whether it was properly installed. I am open to ideas for improving the field. It was not good when they got two combines stuck there this fall.
question_title: How can I fix wet gumbo spots under a pivot when the tile hasn't worked?
expert_answer:
## Why the gumbo spots stay wet

Gumbo is a dense, clay-rich soil with low permeability. Water soaks in slowly and drains slowly, and when it is wet it turns sticky enough to stop a combine. The management on this field adds to the problem. A corn–soybean rotation without cover crops, regular corn residue harvest and repeated tillage to smooth harvest ruts all wear down soil structure and organic matter. Tillage at the same depth year after year can also build a plow pan just below the tilled layer that holds water in the root zone. The pivot then adds water on top, so check the irrigation schedule and amounts on the wet areas to avoid keeping them saturated.

Deep ripping with a bulldozer ripper in the dry 2022 season let you plant and harvest the wet areas, but this year the east spot could not be harvested. Ripping alone is not a reliable fix. University of Minnesota Extension reports that axle loads of 10 tons or more on wet soil can compact soil to 2 feet or deeper, below normal tillage depth, and that deep tillage and freeze-thaw cycles do not reliably remove that compaction.

## Rebuild structure so water can move

- **Reduce tillage.** Less disturbance helps rebuild pore space and infiltration and avoids forming a new plow pan. Subsoil only where it is needed, and carefully, so you do not restart the compaction cycle.
- **Add cover crops after harvest.** Choose species that use enough water in spring to dry the soil for planting and that build structure over time. Cereal rye tolerates heavy, poorly drained soils, many varieties tolerate waterlogging, and rye left growing later in spring draws down soil moisture.
- **Bring in deep roots.** A rotation crop such as alfalfa opens the soil, and as its roots decay they leave channels that carry water and air.
- **Apply manure or compost to the worst areas.** Repeated manure applications raise organic matter, lower bulk density and improve infiltration and water-holding capacity, according to Nebraska Extension.
- **Try a perennial clover in a test area.** Clover grown with the cash crop can cut input costs and add grazing. Set up a trial area before committing the whole field.

## Hold off on re-tiling and moving soil

The current tile never worked, and it may have been installed incorrectly or designed for different soil conditions. Before paying to redo it, give the practices above time to work. If you do re-tile, have it designed and installed by a professional for these soil types. Avoid moving soil from high spots into the wet areas; it strips topsoil quality from where it came from and creates new problems where it lands.

## Measure first, then expand what works

Start with a soil health assessment from a soil specialist. Test organic matter, bulk density and water infiltration in the wet spots and in your better ground so you have a baseline for comparison. Pull past yield maps to see how large the problem areas are and what they cost. Then treat the field as an on-farm research site:

- **This season:** after harvest, cut back tillage, seed cover crops, apply manure or compost to the worst areas and subsoil only where the specialist finds a compacted layer.
- **Next one to two seasons:** run the perennial clover pilot, build a rotation that includes deep-rooted crops and cover crops, and expand the practices that work.
- **After that:** decide whether to move fully to no-till, and reassess whether re-tiling is still needed based on drainage changes.

Recheck bulk density, organic matter and infiltration at regular intervals. Keep a simple log of yields, crop health, and how often and where equipment gets stuck. That record will tell you whether the wet spots are improving and whether new tile is worth the money.

Adapted from a Soil Health Exchange answer first published in CropWatch, University of Nebraska–Lincoln. [Read the original article.](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/2024/soil-health-exchange-addressing-waterlogging-issues-soil-health-management/)

question: Do anhydrous ammonia applications make the soil hard?
question_title: Does anhydrous ammonia make soil hard?
expert_answer:
## Ammonia's effects on soil are brief and local

University of Illinois guidance on corn nitrogen states plainly that there is no basis for the idea that ammonia can make the soil hard. What does cause compaction is running heavy application equipment when soils are moist. The chemical effects of ammonia stay close to the band and fade. Soil pH rises briefly where the ammonia dissolves; Iowa State notes it can climb above 9 at the point of highest concentration before nitrification brings it back down. Microbes are killed in the zone nearest the release point, which Illinois puts at 5 to 8% of the topsoil volume under normal moisture, and they repopulate as the band's ammonium feeds their regrowth.

## Three causes behind the hard feel

- **Compaction from the applicator.** Toolbars and tanks running on wet ground leave denser soil with poorer pore continuity. That is a machinery-and-moisture problem, not an ammonia chemistry problem. University of Minnesota Extension estimates that 70 to 90% of plow-layer compaction happens on the first trip across a field, so a single pass on wet ground does most of the damage.
- **Slot smearing and poor closure.** In wet soil the knife smears the slot walls. Iowa State and Illinois both explain that when the surface later dries, the track can open or crack, and ammonia can move back up it toward the surface.
- **Temporary injury near the band.** Free ammonia is caustic at the injection point and can injure roots and microbes close to the band, especially where soil is dry or the slot sealed poorly. Iowa State notes ammonia moves farther in coarse-textured and low-moisture soils, and Illinois warns that corn planted even several weeks after application can be injured if lighter-textured soil stays dry.

## Read where the hard soil sits

The location of the problem points to its cause:

- Hard **between rows or in wheel tracks**: likely compaction.
- Hard **right along the knife track**: likely smearing or a sealing problem.
- **Poor emergence or pruned roots near the bands**: ammonia placement or timing.

## Set up the next application to avoid it

On Nebraska corn ground, the fixes follow from the diagnosis. Wait until the soil is no longer too wet to carry the rig. Make sure the slot closes well behind the knife. Place ammonia deep enough for the soil texture; Illinois recommends deeper placement on lighter soils to reduce escape and seedling injury. Keep bands away from future seed rows, which Illinois identifies as the most effective protection when RTK guidance lets you place bands between the rows you will plant.

question_title: Has aragonite calcium carbonate been tested as a soil amendment?
expert_answer:
## What aragonite can be expected to do

Aragonite and calcite are two crystal forms of the same compound, CaCO3. Solubility measurements by USGS chemists Plummer and Busenberg show aragonite is slightly more soluble in water than calcite, which could help it react somewhat faster in acidic soil. How fast it actually works in a field will depend on particle size, purity, soil pH, moisture and buffering capacity.

The established benefit is correcting acidity. North Dakota State University's soil fertility guidance explains that low pH changes nutrient solubility, raises aluminum solubility and reduces legume nodulation below pH 5.5, and that lime must be applied at a rate that neutralizes both active and reserve acidity. On neutral, alkaline or calcareous soils, extra carbonate offers little and can hurt: University of Minnesota Extension notes that iron deficiency chlorosis in soybean is more severe in soils with finely divided calcium carbonate.

## Judge it by neutralizing value and fineness

Liming materials are compared by calcium carbonate equivalent (CCE), the acid-neutralizing value relative to pure calcium carbonate, which is set at 100%. Pure aragonite is calcium carbonate, so it has the same theoretical neutralizing value per pound as pure calcite. Any advantage would come from purity, particle size and reaction speed. Virginia Tech Extension combines CCE and fineness into an effective neutralizing value (ENV):

- Fineness factor = [(% passing 20 mesh − % passing 60 mesh) × 0.4] + [(% passing 60 mesh − % passing 100 mesh) × 0.8] + [% passing 100 mesh × 1.0]
- ENV = fineness factor × CCE / 100
- Illustrative example: CCE 100%, with 95% passing 20 mesh, 75% passing 60 mesh and 55% passing 100 mesh, gives a fineness factor of 8 + 16 + 55 = 79 and an ENV of 79%. A soil test calling for 2 tons of pure CaCO3 per acre would need about 2 × 100 / 79 = 2.53 tons of that product.

University of Minnesota Extension states that liming materials applied at equal amounts of effective neutralizing power should have an equal effect on crop yield, so the choice of source comes down mainly to cost. A fine, pure aragonite could need fewer tons per acre than a coarse aglime, and the fair comparison is on an ENV basis.

## Treat strontium as a trace element to monitor

Strontium behaves much like calcium and can compete with it. In a hydroponic study of Chinese cabbage (Qiu and colleagues, 2021), strontium at 1 mmol per liter cut biomass and photosynthesis when calcium was low, and the authors concluded strontium cannot substitute for calcium. A hydroponic rice seedling study (Liu and colleagues, 2023) found low-dose strontium at 0.5 mg per liter eased cadmium toxicity. Neither is field evidence of a crop benefit. Report strontium in the product analysis and track it in soil and tissue tests.

## Design a trial that can test the claims

Place replicated plots on acidic soils with a documented lime requirement, where a response is expected. Compare aragonite with standard calcitic aglime at the same ENV rate, pelletized lime, gypsum where calcium without a pH change is the question, and an untreated check. Measure soil pH and buffer pH, exchangeable calcium, magnesium and potassium, CEC, micronutrients, a microbial respiration measure, infiltration or soil moisture through dry spells, tissue nutrients and yield. Testing the fertilizer-savings claim needs reduced fertilizer rates inside the trial. Supply a lab analysis of CCE, particle-size distribution and strontium with the material.

Soil Health Exchange would welcome replicated data on aragonite and can help connect this question with agronomists in our expert network who could run an independent test.

question: My early-August cover crop mix after sweet corn includes turnips along with sunflower, barley, buckwheat, and medium red clover. Brassicas don't host mycorrhizal fungi. Will the turnips leave fewer of those fungi for next year's crop?
question_title: Will a turnip or radish in my cover crop mix hurt mycorrhizae for next year's crop?
expert_answer:
Question source: a follow-up to a Facebook cover crop discussion, collected by Saurav.

Brassicas don't host arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, or AMF ([see the companion answer](https://soilhealthexchange.com/hub/brassica-root-fungi-without-mycorrhizae)). So it's fair to ask whether turnips leave fewer of these fungi for next year's corn or soybean. A mix with healthy host species typically matches or beats no cover crop for the next crop's AMF. The turnip may trim the hosts' benefit; the documented problems come from a brassica or other non-host that has the field to itself.

AMF on a corn root: round spores and threadlike hyphae. Corn is a mycorrhizal host. Green fluorescence marks glomalin detected with an antibody-based method.Photo: Sara Wright, USDA Agricultural Research Service

## Where the losses come from

The clearest damage follows a non-host grown as the only crop. In Japanese field trials, maize grew much better after sunflower, maize, soybean, or potato than after rapeseed, sugar beet, or fallow, and maize phosphorus uptake and AMF colonization tracked that growth ([Arihara and Karasawa, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1080/00380768.2000.10408760)). A review of University of Guelph maize studies found that after canola, AMF colonization was delayed, early phosphorus uptake fell, and yield could drop ([Miller, 2000](https://doi.org/10.4141/P98-130)). The extreme case is long fallow disorder, which follows more than 12 months without host roots. In soil left fallow for three years, sunflower grown in the glasshouse reached 35% colonization at 72 days, against 80% in soil that had been cropped ([Thompson, 1987](https://doi.org/10.1071/AR9870847)).

These effects hit early and in lean conditions. In northern Japan, the previous-crop effect appeared in dry soils and low-phosphorus soils but not in wet or high-phosphorus soils. In one experiment, maize yields differed by previous crop only where no phosphorus fertilizer was applied. In an earlier field trial, 87 kg P/ha (about 178 lb P2O5 per acre) did not make up the loss after fallow, cabbage, or sugar beet ([Karasawa, 2004](https://www.naro.go.jp/publicity_report/publication/archive/files/naro-se/hoku179summary.pdf)). Part of the dip after canola may have other causes. In one study, maize after canola grew poorly regardless of its colonization, and the effect was gone by the second year of maize ([Koide and Peoples, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11104-012-1237-0)).

## Brassica cover crops in the field

A winter-killed brassica cover behaves differently from a canola crop. In Maryland, across three sites and two years of no-till silage corn, AMF colonization at the four-leaf stage after forage radish never differed from a weed-free check with no cover. Cereal rye raised colonization in three of six site-years. By the eight-leaf stage, the cover crops made no difference at any site ([White and Weil, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11104-009-0131-x)).

Host covers still do more. A meta-analysis pooling 54 field studies found that winter cover crops raised AMF colonization of the following cash crop by 28.5% over winter fallow. Host covers raised it by 30.5%, and non-host covers such as radish, rapeseed, and buckwheat raised it by 17.4% ([Bowles and colleagues, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2664.12815)). In another study, corn after rye or oats was more colonized than corn after canola, radish, or fallow, and higher colonization went with higher plant phosphorus and nitrogen ([Murrell and colleagues, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1742170519000061)).

## Mixes keep the fungi fed

In South Dakota, a five-way fall mix of winter wheat, clover, vetch, turnip, and radish significantly increased soil AMF. The published chart shows about 118 AMF propagules per 100 g of soil after the mix, compared with about 45 without a cover crop ([SDSU Extension and USDA-ARS, 2018](https://midwestcovercrops.b-cdn.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/SD_2018_Fall-Cover-Crops-Boost-Arbuscular-Mycorrhizal-Fungi.pdf)). Compared with no cover, the brassicas did not cancel out the hosts. At one Maryland site, though, a forage radish and rye mix did not raise early corn colonization the way rye alone did, and the researchers suggested the radish may have limited rye's ability to host AMF ([White and Weil, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11104-009-0131-x)). A brassica can trim a host's benefit without erasing it.

Older pot work found little direct suppression. Cabbage, kale, rapeseed, and swede grown beside host plants depressed the hosts' colonization no more than another host plant did ([Ocampo and colleagues, 1980](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8137.1980.tb00746.x)). Living mustard roots can inhibit AMF spore germination in the lab ([Schreiner and Koide, 1993](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8137.1993.tb04536.x)). In the field, the sharpest drop came after Indian mustard was disked in, which cut mycorrhizal inoculum potential by 56.5%; by maize harvest, inoculum potential had risen again in every treatment ([Njeru and colleagues, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13593-013-0197-y)). Radish left to decompose on the surface under no-till showed no drop in the Maryland trials.

## Reading your own mix

Sort the species by host status. Sunflower, barley, and red clover host AMF. Buckwheat is a weak host at best: it is usually classed as non-mycorrhizal, and roots examined in one study carried mainly dark septate endophytes with only occasional arbuscules ([Likar and colleagues, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00572-008-0181-6)). Turnip is the non-host. Three of the five species feed the fungi. Judge the mix by the stand, too: if the turnips smother the barley and clover, the field behaves more like a brassica-only cover.

Timing matters as much as species. In Hokkaido, sunflower sown on August 7 raised AMF colonization and yield of the following maize. Sunflower sown in September or October was barely colonized and gave no benefit, and the researcher concluded that hosts must be sown in August in that climate ([Karasawa, 2004](https://www.naro.go.jp/publicity_report/publication/archive/files/naro-se/hoku179summary.pdf)). An early-August seeding, like this one, falls inside that window; the exact cutoff differs by climate.

## When to plan around a brassica

Pay closer attention when canola, mustard, or sugar beet is the cash crop, or when a brassica-only cover follows a long bare period, especially on dry or low-phosphorus soil. Add a host to the cover. Sunflower or oats sown after cabbage raised colonization and growth of the following maize in Japan, and clover intercropped between cabbage rows raised colonization and yield of the following wheat ([Karasawa and Takebe, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11104-011-1036-z)). In Pennsylvania, oats plus rye beat either species alone for sweet corn colonization, phosphorus uptake, and yield ([Kabir and Koide, 2002](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1014408723664)). Keep phosphorus adequate by soil test, but don't count on fertilizer alone to erase a long non-host stretch; in the Japanese field trial above, it didn't.

To see the effect on your own field, compare strips next season. Look at early corn growth and leaf tissue phosphorus around the five-leaf stage after a host-rich strip and a brassica-heavy strip, then compare yield. Judge by the crop: soil AMF counts respond to fall cover crops, but in a USDA-ARS study those changes were not strongly related to corn performance ([Lehman and colleagues, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00572-019-00884-4)).

question: In lieu of AMF, what do brassica roots associate with below?
question_title: What fungi do brassica roots partner with if not mycorrhizae?
expert_answer:
Question source: a Facebook cover crop discussion, collected by Saurav.

The grower who asked this puts turnips in a fall mix for what they do to soil biology, not to pad the species count. That is the right test for a brassica. Turnip, radish, canola, and mustard roots do host fungi, just not arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF). Their partners are a looser group of root fungi, and some of them move phosphorus into the plant much as AMF do.

## Brassicas left the mycorrhizal partnership behind

The mustard family's ancestors lost the partnership before the family arose. When researchers tested 18 species from the family, none was well colonized. Many of the genes that host plants use to run the partnership were missing from the non-host genomes they compared, including Brassica rapa, the species that includes turnip ([Delaux and colleagues, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1004487)).

AMF can still get into brassica roots, which is where reports of brassica mycorrhizae come from. In Brassica roots, the fungus grew only between dead cells of older roots and built no arbuscules, the structures where a mycorrhizal plant trades sugar for nutrients ([Glenn and colleagues, 1985](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8137.1985.tb03673.x)). When a neighboring host plant fed the fungal network, AMF colonized up to 43% of Arabidopsis root length and cut its growth by more than half ([Veiga and colleagues, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1111/pce.12102)). In a brassica, colonization means contact, not a working trade.

## Helotiales: a real lead from a wild mustard

Helotiales is a large order of fungi. The study behind the interest followed Arabis alpina, a wild alpine relative of mustard, growing in soil with very little available phosphorus (3.7 mg/kg). One Helotiales fungus made up 45% of the fungal DNA in its roots one year and 23% the next. In sterilized native soil, an isolate of that fungus raised shoot biomass by 52% and shoot phosphorus concentration by 61% after 28 days. In split plates, its hyphae carried radioactive phosphorus across a barrier that roots could not cross and delivered it to the plant ([Almario and colleagues, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1710455114)).

That is mycorrhiza-like nutrient delivery, shown across a barrier in lab plates. Researchers writing alongside the study noted that the fungus looked sparse inside roots and that its value in natural conditions still needed testing ([van der Heijden and colleagues, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1716329114)). Six other root fungi from the same study's culture collection slowed root or shoot growth at one or both phosphorus levels ([Almario and colleagues, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1710455114)). The order also includes Sclerotinia, the white mold pathogen of canola. Helotiales names a branch of the fungal tree, not a group of helpers ([Bruyant and colleagues, 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.soilbio.2024.109363)).

## Other root fungi that help when phosphorus is short

Colletotrichum tofieldiae, a root endophyte from wild Arabidopsis in Spain, moved phosphorus into shoots and increased growth and seed production only when phosphorus was scarce. At high phosphate it gave no benefit ([Hiruma and colleagues, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2016.02.028)). In 32-day pot trials with komatsuna, a leafy Brassica rapa, on a phosphorus-fixing volcanic soil, the fungus raised biomass by 53% at the lower dose and more at the higher dose. At low phosphorus, the higher dose nearly tripled phosphorus uptake (+181%); gains were smaller at the higher phosphorus rate ([Sarkodee-Addo and colleagues, 2025](https://doi.org/10.5511/plantbiotechnology.25.0529a)). Strain matters: another strain of the same fungus severely stunts plants ([Hiruma and colleagues, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-40867-w)).

Across these studies, the benefit was largest when phosphorus was short.

## What actually lives in crop brassica roots

Field surveys of canola tell a different story. At three Canadian Prairie sites, the pathogen Olpidium brassicae was the only core fungus in canola roots and averaged about 70% of the fungal DNA sequences there ([Lay and colleagues, 2018](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2018.01188)). Across 37 UK oilseed rape fields, Olpidium was the most abundant root microbe, increased with shorter rotations, and went with lower yields. A different root fungus, Tetracladium, tracked higher yields in the same fields ([Hilton and colleagues, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40168-020-00972-0)).

## Where Trichoderma fits

Trichoderma fungi colonize the roots of many crops, not brassicas in particular. Their link to brassicas is chemical. Brassica tissue releases isothiocyanates as it breaks down, and in a test of 40 Trichoderma isolates, most tolerated brassica seed-meal fumes better than Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium. In the same study, seed meal combined with Trichoderma gave the best control of Pythium disease on sugar beet ([Galletti and colleagues, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocontrol.2008.01.014)). That tolerance makes Trichoderma a workable partner for brassica seed meal.

## What this means for your mix

Give the brassica the jobs it reliably does: fast fall growth, nitrogen capture after harvest, weed suppression through quick canopy, and large taproots that can open channels in the subsoil ([SARE, Managing Cover Crops Profitably](https://www.sare.org/publications/managing-cover-crops-profitably/nonlegume-cover-crops/brassicas-and-mustards/); see [Do radishes and turnips really break up compaction?](https://soilhealthexchange.com/hub/radish-turnip-cover-crops-compaction)). Count fungal partners as a bonus, most likely on soils low in available phosphorus.

Keep a mycorrhizal host growing beside the brassica. Sunflower, barley, and red clover keep AMF fed through fall. A turnip among them may trim that benefit, but it doesn't erase it ([Will a turnip or radish in my mix hurt mycorrhizae for next year's crop?](https://soilhealthexchange.com/hub/brassica-cover-crop-mycorrhizae-next-crop)). For how AMF work and which crops host them, see [What Is AMF?](https://soilhealthexchange.com/blog/what-is-amf)

Give brassicas a break in the rotation. Shorter oilseed rape rotations carried more Olpidium in the UK survey. A brassica cover crop is still a brassica host, so count it when you plan the break between brassica cash crops.

Remember "Helotiales," and pair it with "low phosphorus." Check the field's soil test phosphorus. Where it is low, a turnip's underground company has its best chance to pay its way. Where it is high, expect the brassica's value to come from its growth, roots, and chemistry.

question: Multi-species mixes are planted to enhance diversity. What is diversity and how are we measuring the impact diversity has?
question_title: What is cover crop diversity, and how is it measured?
expert_answer:
Good question — and an important one, because "diversity" gets used loosely in cover crop marketing. There are really two different things hiding under that one word, and telling them apart will save you money. There's also a hard WI reality about whether you can establish a diverse mix at all after grain corn, which I'll get to.

### What "diversity" actually means

**Species diversity** is just how many species are in the mix and how evenly they're represented. Researchers boil this down to one number, the **Shannon index**, which blends richness (how many species) and evenness (how balanced they are). A 12-species blend has high species diversity.

**Functional diversity** is how many distinct \*jobs\* the mix covers — the functional groups. The three standard groups each do something different (SARE 2021):

- **Grasses** (e.g., cereal rye): dense fibrous roots that scavenge leftover nitrogen and build soil organic matter the fastest.
- **Legumes** (e.g., red/crimson clover, hairy vetch): fix atmospheric nitrogen and feed pollinators.
- **Brassicas** (e.g., radish, turnip): large taproots that create biopores and root channels and can improve infiltration (documented relief of measured compaction is variable) and pull up nutrients.

The whole point of mixing across groups is to capture several of those services at once and open up more niches for soil microbes.

### The honest finding: function beats count

The most rigorous regional study on this (11 on-farm sites in SE Nebraska, mixes from 1 to 18 species drawn from six functional groups) found that bumping up species \*count\* alone gave only about a **2.3% biomass effect — not statistically significant** — while adding functional \*groups\* gave roughly a **29% biomass increase**. And critically, no mixture at any site produced more aboveground biomass than the most productive pure stand (Florence et al., PLOS ONE 2019). That 29% comes from a six-functional-group design, not the simplified three-group frame I'm using here to teach the concept — so read it as evidence that \*function matters\*, not as a number tied to a grass/legume/brassica trio. Penn State weed work agrees: cover crop richness reduced weed biomass, but richness explained only about 12% of the variation, and several mixes merely matched — didn't beat — the best single species (Baraibar et al. 2018, Weed Science, doi:10.1017/wsc.2017.59).

Translation: adding a 12th species of the same type buys you almost nothing. Adding a \*different function\* — a legume and a brassica alongside your rye — is what moves the needle, but a simple high-biomass mix can match a fancy diverse one. **Biomass is doing most of the work; diversity is mostly a way to get reliable biomass and a broader set of services.** One caveat to keep front-of-mind: those effect sizes come from SE Nebraska, where legumes and brassicas reliably establish in the fall. WI after grain corn is a different story.

### How impact is measured

On the plant/agronomic side — the things a 1000-acre grower can actually capture (WSU CSANR 2019):

- **Aboveground biomass** (dry-matter lbs/ac, clipped from a known area like a 0.25 m2 quadrat) — the single most predictive metric; most benefits scale with biomass, not species count.
- **Percent green ground cover** — from photos via the free **Canopeo** app.
- **Nutrient uptake** — lab tissue analysis for N, P, K scavenged or fixed.
- **Following corn yield** — yield monitor or weigh wagon; the bottom line.

On the research/soil-biology side, you'll see Shannon and functional-group indices, plus slower lab metrics: microbial biomass and enzyme activity, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) colonization, and soil organic matter fractions. For example, a two-way rye-clover (legume-grass) cover crop increased the transfer of carbon from particulate (POM) into the more stable mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) fraction more than rye or clover alone — but that came from a controlled greenhouse 13C tracer experiment, not a field-yield result (Soil Biology & Biochemistry 2025). These are valuable science but slow and lab-heavy — not where a producer starts.

### What this means for your WI grain-corn ground

Here is the part that changes the practical answer. **UW-Madison Extension explicitly does NOT recommend planting legumes or brassicas after corn grain in Wisconsin** — there aren't enough growing-degree days left in fall for brassicas to provide benefit or for legumes to nodulate and fix N. After grain corn, **cereal rye is the workhorse** (the only reliable option in northern WI; rye or triticale in southern WI), planted by about late October. So a diverse mix \*drilled after harvest\* will largely fail — you'd pay for seed on two species that don't establish.

If you want functional diversity on grain-corn acres, the realistic route is **interseeding into standing corn at about V5-V6 (mid-June)**. A single 2014 season at the Arlington Agricultural Research Station showed rye, red clover, and radish interseeded at V5 establishing without a measured corn yield penalty — but that's one site-year, and interseeded covers can compete with corn for water and light in dry years, so don't read it as an established "no yield penalty" result; your own replicated strip trial is the real test. Interseeding moves your binding constraint from the October harvest window to the June interseeding window — and it requires a modified grain drill or dedicated interseeder, which for 1000 ac is a buy/rent/custom-hire decision to make by spring, not at harvest. Before you commit, confirm your corn herbicide program is compatible (see below) — residual carryover is the usual reason interseeded stands fail.

One more caution worth respecting: WI annual-cropping research found cover crops didn't hurt soybean yield but **some cover crops reduced corn yield** (Agronomy Journal 2022) — which is exactly why a rye-alone control strip matters before you scale anything.

### Bottom line

Don't chase species count. Cover the three functions only where you can actually establish them — which on grain-corn acres means interseeding, not drilling after harvest, and only with a herbicide program that won't kill the mix. Push for biomass, and let a replicated strip trial against rye-alone tell you whether the mix earns its keep on your fields before you scale equipment and seed to 1000 acres.

question: Cover cropping solutions in arid dry land farming. How can we develop cover crop varieties to increase diversity of options in dry land environments, what kind of breeding development would be necessary to facilitate no-till organic in arid environment?
question_title: What breeding would make cover crops work for dryland organic no-till?
expert_answer:
## Water decides what a dryland cover crop can do

Montana State University Extension's summary of its fallow-replacement research (Jones and colleagues, 2022) found that in semi-arid Montana, covers use more soil water than they save by reducing evaporation, even when terminated early. Fields often had 1 to 2.5 inches less soil water in fall than fallow. In water-limited years, wheat after early-terminated covers yielded about 8.6 bu per acre less than after fallow, and about 15.3 bu less after late termination. Where April to July rain exceeded 6.5 inches, yields after covers were not significantly different from fallow. Cover biomass grown after first flower cost about 19 bu of wheat per ton, compared with about 9 bu per ton before flowering.

Timing cuts both ways. In a single-season on-farm trial in southwest Queensland, Australia (Zhang and colleagues, 2023), a late-terminated sorghum cover left 7% less soil water at wheat planting and wheat yielded 61% less, while total and particulate organic carbon rose 17% and 72%. The soil gains are real; the water bill comes due in the next crop.

## Why organic no-till is harder in dry country

Organic no-till depends on a rolled mulch thick enough to smother weeds. Cornell researchers working in New York aim for at least 7,000 lb per acre of cover biomass at termination. Semi-arid Great Plains covers fall far short: a review by Kumar and colleagues (2020) reports cover biomass in southwest Kansas ranging from about 700 lb per acre in a dry year to about 2,400 lb in a wet year. Termination is the second hurdle. In a SARE-funded trial led by Patrick Carr, roller-crimping killed only about 75% of winter rye and triticale at Dickinson, North Dakota, and market crops seeded into the rolled mulch there failed to produce harvestable grain.

## Where breeding would pay off

The Cover Crop Breeding Network, a USDA-funded program working with organic farmers on hairy vetch, winter pea, crimson clover and cereal rye, already selects for weed suppression, early vigor, biomass, winter hardiness, seed yield, soft and non-shattering seed, and early flowering. Dryland organic no-till needs those traits selected under dryland conditions, on dryland sites, with emphasis on:

- **Early biomass on little water.** Montana's data show biomass before flowering costs the next crop far less water than biomass after it, so varieties that build cover fast and flower early fit the water budget.
- **Weed suppression at modest biomass.** Mulch rates that work in humid regions are out of reach in a dry year; competitiveness has to come from earlier, denser canopy rather than tonnage.
- **Termination without herbicide or tillage.** Reliable winterkill or a complete kill from rolling at a predictable growth stage would remove the step that failed at Dickinson.
- **Low weed risk.** Kumar and colleagues report that feral rye, cereal rye gone weedy, causes more than $26 million in annual wheat harvest losses in the western and central US. Non-shattering seed and early, reliable termination keep a cover from becoming next year's weed in a wheat rotation.
- **Nitrogen and protein.** Montana State found wheat protein was often higher after legume covers, with a nitrogen credit of roughly 20 to 30 lb N per acre after one legume cover.

## What you can do now

Use simple mixes: Kumar and colleagues report that a 10-species mix produced no more biomass than single species in eastern Colorado and western Nebraska. Terminate at late bud to first bloom, as Montana State recommends for dry conditions. Measure soil water through the root zone at cover termination and again at cash crop planting beside a fallow strip, and weigh a few clipped cover samples. Two or three seasons of those numbers would show which species fit your rainfall, and they are exactly the data a breeding program needs from dryland farms. The Soil Health Exchange [cover crop selector](https://soilhealthexchange.com/tools/cover-crop-selector) can help narrow the species list for your location.

question: Looking at planting some acres of grass for silage harvest. Annual rye. Whatever. Farmer doesn't want manure on the ground because of his other crops and I just can't see buying fertilizer the way prices are. Is there a blend with clover that will set enough nitrogen to supply the needs of the grass? Or am I dreaming?
question_title: Can clover reduce nitrogen fertilizer purchases for grass silage?
expert_answer:
Question source: Everything Cover Crops Facebook group, collected by Saurav.

Clover can lower purchased nitrogen for a grass–clover silage crop because the legume produces forage using fixed nitrogen. Supplying the grass component is a separate budget: nitrogen held in clover tissue becomes available as that tissue breaks down. The first-cut deadline matters especially in a newly seeded mixture.

## Count the clover as part of the crop

Clover and its root-nodule bacteria fix nitrogen that supports the clover's own growth. That gives you forage to harvest while the grass uses soil nitrogen. Some fixed nitrogen also reaches companion grasses through turnover and decomposition of legume tissues. The size and timing of that contribution depend on the stand. [Minnesota Extension](https://extension.umn.edu/agriculture/crop-production/forages/benefits-of-legume-grass-mixtures) explains how legumes and grasses complement each other.

UK guidance from [AHDB](https://ahdb.org.uk/knowledge-library/manure-and-slurry-for-clover) reports that a good grass–clover stand containing 30–40% clover in its dry matter can produce an annual dry-matter yield comparable to pure grass receiving about 180 kg nitrogen per hectare. This comparison describes whole-stand production over a season; the amount to budget for a new silage planting depends on its growing window and local conditions.

This makes the amount of clover in the harvested forage a central management decision. For example, [Penn State's first-cut forage guidance](https://extension.psu.edu/first-cut-forage-considerations) advises against adding nitrogen when legumes make up more than half the stand. Use your regional guidance for the species, stand age, and yield goal. Measure the crop's actual composition through the season; the percentage of clover seed in a bag does not tell you its eventual share of forage dry matter.

## How clover nitrogen reaches the grass

Fixed nitrogen is built into clover leaves, stems, roots, and nodules. When clover is terminated and its residues stay in the field, microbial decomposition releases part of that nitrogen for subsequent uptake. Temperature, moisture, residue composition, and placement affect the timing. [SARE’s guidance on nitrogen release](https://www.sare.org/publications/managing-cover-crops-profitably/building-soil-fertility/) explains this process. Termination starts a residue-management phase; release continues as decomposition proceeds.

Some nitrogen can also reach grass while the clover stand remains alive, through root and nodule turnover and compounds released by roots. A [tracer study in a young clover–ryegrass model pasture](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9705487/) identified root exudation and decomposition as transfer pathways, with low overall transfer in that experimental system. [Texas A&M’s forage guidance](https://overton.tamu.edu/faculty-staff/gerald-wayne-evers/cool-season-legumes/nitrogen-fixation/) also describes the importance of decomposing legume material.

For a new silage planting, budget grass nitrogen from soil supply, previous-crop credits, and any planned inputs against the first-cut deadline. Keep the estimate of total nitrogen fixed by clover separate from the amount expected to reach the grass before that harvest.

## Choose the blend around the harvest window

First clarify what you mean by annual rye. Cereal rye and annual or Italian ryegrass have different growth patterns, winter survival, and harvest uses. Even ryegrass cultivars differ in heading and regrowth. [Nebraska Extension's rye and ryegrass guide](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/2019/which-one-do-i-want-rye-or-ryegrass/) explains the distinction.

For a cool-season silage stand kept for multiple cuts, red clover with a locally adapted companion grass is a useful starting point. Italian or hybrid ryegrass with red clover is an established option in suitable climates; [AHDB's red-clover guidance](https://ahdb.org.uk/knowledge-library/how-to-use-red-clover) describes its use in short forage rotations. Match the grass cultivar and clover to local winters, summer moisture, and your cutting schedule. For a short annual crop, an annual clover such as berseem or crimson may fit the growing window better, depending on region and planting date. [Wisconsin Extension](https://dairy.extension.wisc.edu/articles/basics-of-cocktail-forage-mixes/) describes these annual-forage options.

Have the supplier specify forage varieties, pure live seed rates, and an establishment plan that gives the clover room to grow. Inoculate for the legume species you choose. [Maine's red-clover guidance](https://extension.umaine.edu/publications/2259e/) covers nodulation, establishment, and cutting management. The right blend is the one that produces enough legume at the time you intend to harvest.

## Budget for what leaves in the silage wagon

Cutting a regrowing clover stand for silage removes forage while leaving the plants alive. Much of the nitrogen in the cut material leaves in the wagon. That fixed nitrogen has already helped produce the harvested clover feed, while roots and stubble remain for further cycling. A following-crop credit should reflect the residues actually retained: [SARE’s soil-fertility guidance](https://www.sare.org/publications/managing-cover-crops-profitably/building-soil-fertility/) explains why harvesting a legume reduces its residual nitrogen contribution compared with leaving it as green manure.

Clover also needs suitable pH, phosphorus, potassium, and other essential nutrients to grow and fix nitrogen. Soil-test before sowing and account for the nutrients removed in repeated cuts. Keeping manure off this field is compatible with a clover-based plan, but deficiencies still need a source. Use the soil report to decide which purchases matter. [Maine's red-clover guidance](https://extension.umaine.edu/publications/2259e/) connects fertility with establishment and persistence.

## Start with a strip you can measure

Before committing all the acres, try the proposed mixture on a manageable strip. At each cut, record dry-matter yield, clover share, and forage quality, along with seed, establishment, fertility, and harvest costs. Check nodulation on several clover plants and use a harvest and wilting plan suited to the mixture and storage system. Compare cost per ton of usable dry matter so differences in moisture do not distort the result. The nitrogen saving needs to cover any added costs while delivering the feed you need.

Illustration of biomass sampling with a quadrat. For a grass–clover trial, separate the grass and clover fractions and measure their dry matter. Soil Health Exchange editorial illustration (AI-assisted), reused from A Practical Guide to Choosing Fall Cover Crops.

The details needed to choose a blend are your location, planting date, first-cut deadline, number of planned cuts, previous crop, soil report, and intended livestock. With those in hand, you can build a realistic plan for a crop in which clover supplies a meaningful part of the feed and reduces the nitrogen bill.

question: A south-central Illinois grower is looking for the same humic-product strips followed over many seasons. What benefits could a grower count on after ten years of applying the product to the same ground?
question_title: What can you expect after ten years of applying humic products?
expert_answer:
## What the same-field trials found

USDA researchers kept plots in the same positions for five crop seasons in an Iowa corn–soybean rotation. One humic product significantly increased yield in six of ten comparisons with untreated plots. Rates and timing changed partway through, and a nearby field responded less consistently. A USDA meeting abstract described small improvements in a few soil physical measurements after five years of application.

## Measure the crop and the soil separately

Commercial humic products can be made from materials such as lignite. Formulations vary and may include added fertilizer. Soil organic matter includes many forms of carbon already in the field, including residues, microbial material and carbon associated with minerals. A change in crop growth or nutrient uptake in the application year tells you how the crop responded. For a claim about lasting soil carbon, measure the carbon in a defined amount of soil over time. For an aggregation claim, measure aggregate stability directly.

## Keep the same check strips

Mark several treated and untreated pairs with GPS and keep them through the rotation. Match fertilizer and field operations across strips, and account for any nutrients in the product. Record the formulation, rate and cost. Record soil texture and pH at the start. Take paired soil samples and use the same sampling season and depth on return visits. If carbon is the goal, measure bulk density and compare stocks on an equivalent soil-mass basis. If you track microbial activity, use the same respiration test under comparable moisture and temperature conditions. To measure persistence, set aside replicated strips where you stop applying the product after several seasons and track those alongside the strips that stay treated and the original checks.

At each harvest, compare yield adjusted to the same grain moisture. Multiply the yield difference by your grain price and subtract the product and application cost per acre. That gives you a result you can use this year while the longer soil record builds.

question: A southwestern Ontario no-tiller wants to broadcast oats, possibly with radish, into standing corn around August. Could the roots help carry harvest equipment in a wet fall and protect the soil without leaving a cold, wet seedbed for 15-inch soybeans?
question_title: Can oats seeded into standing corn help carry a wet harvest?
expert_answer:
## First see whether the oats establish

Oats can give you a fibrous root mat and ground cover if enough plants come up before corn harvest. Broadcasting into standing corn depends on seed reaching the ground, getting rain and having enough light under the canopy. Check the corn herbicide program for restrictions and the chance of carryover. Ontario interseeding research found that several residual herbicides reduced cover establishment, although those trials used earlier, drilled interseeding. Test oats alone first. Add a third strip with oats and radish if you want to see whether radish changes the stand or spring residue.

## Read rutting and compaction separately

Ruts tell you how the surface handled a pass. Heavy axle loads can still compact wet soil below the root mat even where surface ruts are shallow. Use fixed lanes where practical and keep loads lower when the field is marginal. If the ground is too wet, wait or unload at the edge.

Leave several no-cover strips alongside the oats on similar ground. Record stand and ground cover before harvest. Along already planned passes on trafficable ground, record rut depth and soil moisture at the same depth on the same day. Compare similar axle loads, tire pressures and numbers of passes. The useful result is whether the oats repeatedly reduce rutting under comparable conditions.

## Check the soybean row in spring

Ontario guidance treats oats and forage radish as usually winter-killed in an after-wheat cover crop. Scout in spring for survivors and plan termination if needed. Check soil temperature and moisture at soybean seeding depth and note whether residue mats or pushes into the slot. Compare the soybean stand across strips. Carry the practice to more acres if the fall cover is worth having and your planter still gets an even stand.
