question: I'm considering cover crops and no-till on 800 acres of corn-soy. What will it cost me during the transition, when will I see returns, and what's the total economic case including reduced input costs?
question_title: When do cover crops and no-till start paying on an Iowa corn-soybean farm?
expert_answer:
## What the transition costs on 800 acres

Expect added costs in the first few years for cover crop seed, which varies widely with species or mix; establishment, whether fuel and planting or aerial seeding; termination, typically herbicide in a no-till system; and equipment changes such as no-till planter setup. SARE's 2019 cover crop economics bulletin, built on a national farmer survey, used a median of $25 per acre for seed and $12 for hired seeding, or $37 per acre. Cereal seed can run as little as $5 to $10 an acre, complex legume mixes up to $50, and aerial seeding $12 to $18. At $37 an acre, 800 acres comes to about $29,600 a year. Spring termination adds $10 to $12 an acre if you are not already making a burndown pass.

Herbicide choice depends on the cover crop species and growth stage. In no-till, terminate the cover before it reaches reproductive stages, or it becomes hard to control and can interfere with planting the cash crop.

## What comes back, and when

In the first one to three years, some producers see yield variability or slight reductions while management is still being worked out; this usually improves as the system settles. Iowa State trials show where that risk sits: corn following a rye cover crop yielded 5% less across five research farms in 2009 to 2013 and about 2% less in later trials with early termination, while soybean yields were unaffected by rye. Most measurable benefits arrive after three to five years, depending on soil, climate and consistency: better soil structure and water infiltration and retention, less erosion and runoff, gradual gains in nutrient cycling and fertilizer use efficiency, and more resilience to drought and heavy rain, which steadies yields.

Some offsets start in year one. If you now chisel in the fall and field-cultivate twice in spring, SARE valued dropping those passes at about $24 an acre, or roughly $19,000 a year on 800 acres. SARE noted that the basic NRCS EQIP payment for cover crops started at $50 an acre or more in most Corn Belt states in 2019; check current Iowa rates with your NRCS office. Iowa's Crop Insurance Discount Program takes $5 an acre off the next year's premium for fall-planted covers, for acres not enrolled in another state or NRCS cost-share program.

## How the budget adds up over five years

SARE's corn budget, at $3.50 corn and 200 bushels, put the net return from cover crops alone at about minus $31 an acre in year one, plus $1 in year three and plus $18 in year five, before cost-share. Adding the no-till savings moved those figures to minus $7, plus $25 and plus $42. For soybeans with no-till, the figures were about $0, plus $24 and plus $34. Those budgets assume fertilizer savings that build to 30 lb of N per acre by year five. Iowa-specific numbers are tougher: Iowa State economists surveying Iowa farmers found average annual net returns to cover crops were consistently negative unless the covers were grazed or harvested for forage, and the farmers who came out ahead usually also received cost-share.

Over the long term, many producers find the combined system economically competitive with, or more profitable than, conventional systems, especially under variable weather. The way to know on your own ground is to keep your own budget. For each field, record seed, seeding and termination costs, the tillage passes you dropped, cost-share received and yields from strips with and without covers, and compare the totals each year from year one through year five.

question: I'm applying feedlot manure on irrigated corn ground in south-central Nebraska. My neighbor says I can cut synthetic fertilizer entirely if I apply enough manure. Is that true, and what's the catch with cover crops in the mix?
question_title: Can feedlot manure replace all the commercial fertilizer on irrigated corn?
expert_answer:
## Why a full nitrogen rate overloads phosphorus

Your neighbor may be right that it can be done, but it is not always the most economical plan. Applying enough manure to meet any one nutrient's need can put on excess amounts of the others, nutrients that would do more good spread over more fields, holding down fertilizer inputs across the whole farm rather than on one field.

Beef manure is the classic case. Some of its nitrogen is lost as ammonia during handling, spreading and composting, which leaves more phosphorus for every pound of nitrogen. University of Nebraska–Lincoln (UNL) Extension's feedlot guide finds that annual nitrogen-based applications over-apply phosphorus by three to six times, and potassium builds up as well. The excess is larger when the feedlot feeds ingredients high in phosphorus, such as distillers grains: a finishing diet with 40% wet distillers grains carries about 0.55% phosphorus, well above what cattle need. If you would rather apply only two or three years' worth of phosphorus with the manure, plan to add nitrogen fertilizer to cover the rest of the crop's need.

## Test the manure before setting a rate

Different manures carry different proportions of nutrients, so a manure analysis before application is always recommended to choose an appropriate rate. Book values give only an average; UNL notes that the actual nitrogen and phosphorus content can be determined only by laboratory analysis, and that roughly half of feedlot manure nitrogen is typically usable in the first year. Pair the manure analysis with a current soil test so the rate fits both the crop's need and what is already in the field.

## How a rye cover crop changes the timing

The catch with cover crops depends on which one you grow. In much of Nebraska that is cereal rye, which is very good at scavenging and taking up nutrients left in the soil. As the cover crop decomposes, it releases those nutrients back to the soil, where they become available to the next crop, just as crop residues do.

Speed depends on the carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio. Corn residue breaks down more slowly than soybean residue, and covers with a higher C:N ratio break down more slowly than those with a lower one. USDA NRCS explains that soil microbes need a diet near 24:1; residue above that ties up soil nitrogen for a time, and residue below it releases nitrogen. NRCS lists rye at about 26:1 in the vegetative stage and 37:1 at flowering, corn stover at 57:1 and beef manure at 17:1, so rye left to grow tall releases its nutrients more slowly. In Iowa State measurements, 60% to 77% of the nitrogen in rye residue had left the residue 105 days after spring termination.

Mineralization also depends heavily on weather. The microbes that break down residue and manure need moisture and warmth, so more happens in warm or irrigated summers than in dry areas or in winter. On irrigated ground in south-central Nebraska, that works in your favor during the growing season.

If you need help working out a manure rate that meets your crop's needs, bring your manure analysis and soil test to your local Nebraska Extension office or contact Leslie Johnson; they will be happy to help.

question: I planted cereal rye cover before corn. How much nitrogen credit do I get, when does it become available, and how should I adjust my fertilizer program?
question_title: How much nitrogen credit do I get from cereal rye before corn?
expert_answer:
## Rye biomass and termination timing set the risk

The answer depends on how much rye you grew and when you terminated it. With a lot of biomass, rye can tie up nitrogen, and depending on conditions you may see an N penalty almost immediately. If rye biomass reaches 1,000 lb per acre, consider starter nitrogen and/or sulfur applied near the row at planting. Terminating when rye is less than 8 inches tall reduces the risk of N immobilization and lost corn yield potential. Brassica mixes carry less risk of N tie-up than cereal rye.

Expect a small yield drag on average, with a lot of variation. Across five Iowa State research farms in 2009 to 2013, corn after rye yielded 5% less than corn without it, and the gap grew as rye biomass increased. In later Iowa State trials where rye was terminated at 6 to 8 inches, the gap narrowed to about 2%.

## Where starter nitrogen fits

In Iowa State trials at four research farms in 2014 and 2015, 30 lb of starter N per acre placed 2 inches beside and 2 inches below the seed raised corn yield by 3 bu/ac on average, and by 7 to 14 bu/ac in three of six site-years. The researchers concluded that with early rye termination, starter N can offset the rye's negative yield effect in tilled or no-till systems, and that the higher 30 lb rate is especially useful if you plan to sidedress most of your N.

That work is still developing. When Iowa State added a third year, starter N on its own no longer significantly changed yield. Purdue University trials at three sites tested 0 to 75 lb of starter N after rye and found it raised early-season N uptake but had an inconsistent effect on yield. Iowa State also found the economic optimum N rate was nearly the same with and without rye, only 6 lb per acre apart, so the adjustment is mainly in timing and placement rather than total rate.

## When the rye nitrogen comes back

Rye aboveground biomass often holds 20 to 60 lb of N per acre; Iowa State measured an average of 20 lb, ranging from 2 to 62. That nitrogen returns slowly. In Iowa State residue-bag studies, 60% of rye N following corn and 77% following soybean had left the residue 105 days after spring termination, so treat it as a season-long supply rather than a credit you can subtract at planting.

Disease pressure is another factor in the rye-to-corn transition. In Iowa field trials published in 2023, rye terminated 3 days before planting produced 2.1 times more biomass and 4.1% less corn yield than rye terminated 14 days before planting, and broadcast rye was linked to more seedling root rot and Pythium than drilled rye.

Before you terminate next spring, estimate rye biomass against the 1,000 lb mark and note its height. Leave a few strips without starter, and compare their yield with the starter strips at harvest to see what the starter is worth on your fields.

question: What have people done for interseeding into corn?
question_title: How do farmers interseed cover crops into growing corn?
expert_answer:
## Why interseeding fits Illinois corn

The median first killing freeze arrives in mid to late October in northwest and central Illinois, and in late October or early November in southern and northeast Illinois, according to the Illinois State Climatologist. Once corn comes off, a cover seeded after harvest has little time to grow. Interseeding puts the cover into the living crop in early summer so it is already in place at harvest. On fields harvested early, especially in southern Illinois, drilling after harvest may still work; the Midwest Cover Crops Council selector tool, which University of Illinois Extension points growers to, shows recommended planting windows by location.

## Pick the corn stage and the species

University of Wisconsin–Madison reports success from V3 to V7, and most of its research seeds at V5. Penn State work summarized by GROW found V4 to V5 gave the best cover emergence, and early interseeding at V3 to V4 in 30-inch rows gave the best weed suppression. In South Dakota State trials, seeding at corn planting or very early tended to reduce corn yield, while seeding after V4 generally did not. Expect the cover to germinate and then sit under the canopy; grass survival depends on how much light reaches it. Judge the stand by ground cover after harvest, not by what you see in July.

- **Red clover:** drilled at 12 lb/ac about ¼ inch deep into V5 corn with no significant grain yield difference in Wisconsin trials. It overwinters, so plan a spring termination.
- **Annual ryegrass:** a reliable choice on Wisconsin farms. Plan its spring kill as well.
- **Cereal rye:** did not always survive to fall harvest in Wisconsin, and tended to reduce corn yield in South Dakota trials.
- **Radish:** makes very little root below ground when interseeded, so do not count on a taproot effect.
- **Mixes:** in South Dakota, mixes of four or more species produced the most fall biomass without reducing yield. Buckwheat, berseem clover, hairy vetch and winter camelina tended to reduce corn yield.

## Residual herbicides and seeding method make or break the stand

Herbicide injury depends on the product and the cover species. In trials at eight Pennsylvania, Maryland and New York site-years, mesotrione cut red clover biomass by 80%, while atrazine, saflufenacil and rimsulfuron did not reduce it. S-metolachlor, pyroxasulfone, pendimethalin and dimethenamid-P reduced annual ryegrass; acetochlor did not. Those trials were on silt loam soils, so pull every label you applied this year and read the rotational planting restrictions. South Dakota State advises against applying a product whose label keeps a species out for the following year or 18 months if you plan to interseed it. For next season, GROW recommends a shorter-lived residual before emergence and no residual in the postemergence pass.

Drilling gives better establishment and biomass than broadcasting but costs more. Broadcasting into corn has been difficult, especially in dry soil. If you broadcast, South Dakota State recommends a 15 to 25% higher seeding rate than drilled. Keep 30-inch rows: Penn State trials in 60-inch rows gave covers more light, but corn yields fell about 32% for determinate hybrids and 23% for flex-ear hybrids.

Next step: choose one field whose herbicide program is compatible with the cover. Drill red clover or annual ryegrass at V4 to V5 in several strips, and leave untreated check strips beside them. Record the herbicides, seeding date, seeding rate and rain in the week after seeding. After harvest, measure ground cover in each strip and compare corn yield on paired strips. Take the results to your University of Illinois Extension educator when you plan a larger program.

question: I farm clay loam in central Iowa with a corn-soy rotation. What cover crop species or mix should I plant after corn harvest in mid-October, and will it establish before freeze-up?
question_title: What cover crop should I plant after mid-October corn harvest in central Iowa, and will it establish before freeze-up?
expert_answer:
## Why cereal rye fits a late slot ahead of soybeans

The Midwest Cover Crops Council's Iowa recipe for fields coming out of corn and going to soybean is cereal rye. Its seeding deadline is two weeks after the average 28°F hard frost: October 21 in northern Iowa, October 28 in central Iowa and November 7 in southern Iowa. Plant as soon after harvest as you can. Rye germinates in soil as cool as 34°F and is among the most reliable cover crops for overwintering in Iowa. Oats and radish are common too, but they winterkill, and Iowa State Extension advises shifting toward cereal rye the later seeding gets.

## How much to expect before freeze-up

A late seeding gives a thin fall stand. In a 2018–2019 Practical Farmers of Iowa trial on seven farms, rye seeded after soybean harvest for the following corn crop made very little biomass overall because of late seeding and a cool, wet fall. Seeding later cut biomass at five of six farms, and cutting the rate from 55 to 28 lb/ac cut it at five of seven. Neither seeding date nor rate changed corn yield or the soil health test results. A modest late stand is still worth having, so seed your earliest-harvested fields first and give them the full rate.

## Seeding rate, depth and method

- **Drilled:** 55 lb/ac at 0.75 to 1.5 inches deep, assuming better than 85% germination (MCCC). The minimum rate in the recipe is 45 lb/ac.
- **Broadcast with shallow incorporation:** 61 lb/ac, worked in less than 1.5 inches (MCCC).
- **Aerial or broadcast without incorporation:** less dependable than drilling. The NRCS–Iowa State fact sheet lists 55 lb/ac of pure live seed for aerial seeding, against 45 drilled.
- **Overseeding into standing corn:** Iowa State Extension advises seeding just ahead of a good rain, and switching to post-harvest seeding if the forecast stays dry.

On a large acreage, map your expected harvest order before the combine rolls and work out how many acres your drill can reach by October 28 as fields come open. If the numbers fall short, add a second drill or hire a custom seeder, and keep aerial seeding for the acres you cannot reach in time.

## Spring termination ahead of soybeans

Iowa State's 2023 termination review found that 0.75 lb acid equivalent per acre of glyphosate should kill small rye, under 18 inches, in favorable conditions; the older 1 lb rate is generous. Spray on a sunny day above 60°F, ideally with a forecast that stays above 40°F for three to five days, and add clethodim for difficult conditions. Timing is less critical before soybean than before corn, but kill the rye before the beans emerge. For crop insurance, the NRCS termination guidelines split Iowa between two zones: in Zone 3, terminate at or before planting; in Zone 4, before crop emergence. No-till systems can delay termination up to seven days past the zone deadline. Confirm your zone and current rules with your crop insurance agent before planting green.

Cost-share helps with seed and seeding costs. For 2026, the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship offers $30 per acre for first-time cover crop users and $20 per acre for returning users, on up to 160 acres per participant, through county Soil and Water Conservation District offices. Ask the same office about NRCS programs, and get a current seed quote before you set your acreage.

question: I want to reduce glyphosate use for terminating cover crops. Can roller-crimping work at scale in my region? What about winterkill species?
question_title: Reducing Cover-Crop Herbicide Use in Nebraska: Three Lanes, Measured Before Scaling
expert_answer:
## The decision is not “herbicide or no herbicide”

On 5,000 acres, the practical goal is to reduce routine herbicide use where biology, rotation, and field capacity make that reduction dependable—while keeping a rescue option where the cover or weeds do not cooperate. Nebraska data support three different lanes: roller-crimp mature cereal covers mainly ahead of soybean; use winter-killed covers after an early harvest; and treat early corn interseeding as a measured trial, not as the default for every acre.

🌱

#### Nebraska evidence at a glance

UNL recommends at least 8,000 lb/ac of dry cereal-cover biomass (about 4–5 ft tall), drilled at 100 lb/ac or more in mid- to late September in eastern Nebraska, and crimped at flowering. In 2020 interseeding trials, check corn averaged 214 bu/ac versus 209 bu/ac with interseeding. Across the 2019–2022 dataset, interseeding reduced corn yield in 6 of 12 site-years and reduced marginal return in 10 of 12; weather, herbicide carryover, irrigation, and canopy opening strongly affected those outcomes.

## Lane 1: roller-crimp where the system can make a mat

The strongest first fit is a named cereal rye or triticale variety ahead of soybean. UNL’s Nebraska guidance calls for at least about 8,000 lb/ac of dry matter, or 4–5 ft of height, from a stand drilled at 100 lb/ac or more in mid- to late September in eastern Nebraska. Biomass makes the weed-suppressing mat; maturity determines whether the crimper can terminate the plant.

🌱

#### Crimp at anthesis—not merely when rye has headed

Anthesis is flowering: yellow anthers are visibly extending from the rye heads and shedding pollen. In the Zadoks cereal-growth scale, anthesis begins at stage 61. A peer-reviewed rye study found consistent roller-crimper control at this stage because mature reproductive stems are much less likely to stand back up and regrow after being crushed. Crimping at boot or heading can flatten rye temporarily but often allows recovery; waiting well past flowering improves maturity but increases the chance of viable seed. Because a field does not mature all at once, confirm that most of the stand—not just the earliest plants—has reached anthesis.

- Pilot one field with at least three paired strips: the farm’s current termination program beside crimping. Keep variety, population, fertility, and harvest method the same.
- Measure dry biomass before crimping, maturity stage, ground coverage, green regrowth 7–10 days later, weed escapes by species, rescue-treated acres, and moisture-corrected soybean yield.
- Set the rescue rule before planting. A targeted postemergence treatment is risk management, not a failed trial; its acres, product, application, and yield belong in the comparison.

Before scaling, use the acres per hour measured during the pilot—not a paper estimate—to confirm the crimper can finish the target acres while most of the cover is at anthesis without delaying soybean planting. Include turns, transport, refilling, a possible second pass, and available operator hours in that workload check.

## Lane 2: remove spring termination after an early harvest

After wheat, silage, seed corn, or another early harvest, a winter-killed mixture can remove a planned spring burndown where it establishes well. The MCCC/UNL Nebraska recipe combines, per acre, 16–24 lb oats + 4 lb forage sorghum or sorghum-sudangrass + 2 lb pearl millet + 1 lb grain sorghum + 1 lb rapeseed + 4 lb buckwheat. Together those components make one 28–36 lb/ac mixed-species recipe; the rates are not six alternative monocrop rates. Oats also help carry the smaller seeds through the drill.

ℹ️

#### Here, 0.5 inch means planting depth

The recipe is drilled about one-half inch deep—not irrigated with one-half inch of water. Rapeseed is the smallest-seeded component, so it limits how deep the whole mixture should be placed; planting the mixture much deeper can reduce emergence of that component. Uniform wheat-residue spreading, seed-to-soil contact, and seeding immediately after harvest are still important, especially when the top half-inch is drying.

A farmer can use one winter-killed species instead of the full mixture, but should then use that species’ Nebraska-specific monocrop seeding rate and management—not the smaller component rate shown above. For example, 1 lb/ac rapeseed in this recipe is its contribution to a mixture, not a stand-alone recommendation. Use the MCCC selector or local Extension guidance to size a single-species rate and to check forage, herbicide, and wheat-curl-mite considerations.

## Lane 3: interseed corn only where the farm can control establishment

UNL’s 2019–2022 on-farm work used a drill between rows at V3–V5. The result was not a simple success or failure. Corn yield was lower with interseeding in 6 of 12 site-years, and marginal return was lower in 10 of 12 after seed and seeding costs. The economic calculation did not include grazing, incentives, or unpriced future soil benefits. At the same time, seven of ten 2020–2021 corn sites were affected by a wind event, two 2022 sites were lost to hail, and two were abandoned because residual herbicide interfered with the covers. Those limitations make the data a warning about execution and risk—not proof that every interseeded acre loses money.

The clearest single-year signal was 2020: check corn averaged 214 bu/ac and interseeded corn 209 bu/ac (p = 0.001); four of six sites had significantly lower yield and five of six had lower net return. In 2019, two sites had no yield difference, although their interseeded treatments still had lower net return.

- Drill at V3–V4 where possible—UNL’s preferred target is V3—for seed-to-soil contact before the corn canopy closes. Select only fields whose preemergence products and plant-back restrictions fit every species in the mixture.
- Budget establishment water in a dry spring. In this section, a 0.5-inch pivot application means the depth of water applied after interseeding—not seed depth. UNL reported that one or two 0.5-inch applications may be needed to wet the shallow seed zone and support emergence when rainfall is absent; actual need still depends on soil moisture, texture, residue, and forecast.
- Record hybrid canopy, wind or hail opening, September cover and weed biomass, post-harvest grazing days, water applied, and any incentive actually received. These are the variables needed to explain the return.
- The three-year sampling did not detect differences between interseeded and check strips in the measured soil-health or nutrient indicators. Because treatment replications were composited within each site, small changes would have been difficult to detect. Interpret this as “no measured short-term change in this dataset,” not as proof that longer-term changes cannot occur; base the near-term acreage decision on establishment, yield, cost, grazing, and other benefits the farm actually measures.

### Which species fit early interseeding into Nebraska corn?

🌱

#### A simple three-species starting point

UNL’s simplest recommendation is annual or Italian ryegrass + red clover + forage collards. The ryegrass provides fibrous roots, nitrogen scavenging, and dependable overwintering in the Nebraska trials; red clover stays relatively low, fixes nitrogen, and can overwinter; forage collards emerge quickly, cover the ground, and can add grazing value. UNL did not publish one universal rate for this simplified mix, so set rates for the drill, seed lot, herbicide program, grazing goal, and acceptable seed cost rather than copying a research mixture blindly.

Add species only for a specific goal. Buckwheat, cowpeas, and brassicas provide quick early shade for weed suppression; cowpeas, beans, hairy vetch, and clovers add legumes; annual/Italian ryegrass and other grasses emphasize erosion control and N scavenging; collards, turnips, radishes, ryegrass, and clovers fit a forage goal. UNL cautions that red-ripper cowpea became too aggressive and set seed, yellow sweetclover was difficult to terminate, buckwheat can set seed in a corn–soybean rotation, and low-rate cereal rye had spotty winter survival. Every species must also fit the preceding herbicide label and the next crop.

## Manage nitrogen by cover type and timing—not by one universal add-on

Cereal rye is a proven nitrogen scavenger—that is a benefit for reducing nitrate loss, and also the reason young corn may need protected access to starter N. Nebraska studies summarized by UNL found 1,312–2,073 lb/ac of rye biomass containing 34–54 lb N/ac. That N is held in rye tissue, not immediately lost, but mature high-C:N residue releases it slowly. In a decomposition study cited by UNL, rye released less than 10 lb N/ac during the first four weeks after corn planting. During that period, microbes decomposing rye can also compete with corn for soil N.

For corn following cereal rye, the clear starting recommendation is 30–50 lb of actual N/ac at or near planting, placed with an agronomically safe starter method such as a 2×2 band, and counted inside the field’s total seasonal N plan. Example: if the adjusted whole-season plan is 180 lb N/ac and 40 lb is placed as starter, about 140 lb remains for the planned later applications—not 180 plus an extra 40. A three-site Indiana study found that 50 or 75 lb starter N/ac increased yield by 18.3 bu/ac at one site but did not change yield at two sites. That variability supports protecting early N access while using Nebraska recommendations, soil and water credits, and in-field strips to decide total rate; it does not support increasing total N automatically on every rye acre.

ℹ️

#### Make the break-even visible

Net change/ac = yield difference × crop price + avoided herbicide and application + grazing or incentive value actually captured − seed, seeding, crimping, rescue treatment, added water, labor, and equipment ownership. Allowable yield loss (bu/ac) = net non-yield benefit/ac ÷ crop price. Calculate each lane separately; a whole-farm average can hide a practice that works only after early harvest or only ahead of soybean.

## Use an expansion rule that can survive a difficult year

1. Use at least three side-by-side repetitions and harvest treatments separately. One strip can be confounded by soil, drainage, or a yield-monitor lag.
2. Predefine agronomic gates: acceptable stand, no unmanaged weed or volunteer-grain problem, completion inside the planting window, and no statistically or economically important yield penalty.
3. Expand after two seasons only if net return is competitive once every rescue acre and labor hour is included. A grazing or conservation goal can justify a known cost, but label that payment or value explicitly.
4. Stop or redesign a lane when the same failure repeats—for example, insufficient biomass for crimping, unavailable establishment water, incompatible residual herbicides, or a workload that delays planting.

## Bottom line

- Ahead of soybean with a heavy rye or triticale stand: crimp when most plants are at anthesis and keep a rescue plan.
- After wheat or another early harvest: use the entire winter-killed mixture at its combined rate, drilled about 0.5 inch deep—or select one species and use its separate monocrop rate.
- Into V3–V4 corn: start with annual/Italian ryegrass, red clover, and forage collards, then add species only for a defined goal and compatible herbicide program.
- When corn follows cereal rye: place 30–50 lb actual N/ac near planting as part of the total seasonal N program.

Pilot each lane in replicated strips. Expand only the lanes that fit the planting window and protect crop stand, weed control, yield, labor, and net return on this operation.

question:
It seems everyone has a soil health product for sale these days, so I find it hard to sort through and select any amendment or biostimulant with confidence. Is there any independent research concerning biostimulants, humates, etc? I'm in northeast Nebraska, in Pierce, Antelope, and Knox counties. Corn and soybeans. Lots of sandy ground.
Thank you.
question_title: Is there independent research showing biostimulants or humic products pay for corn and soybeans?
expert_answer:
## What Nebraska trials found

The Nebraska On-Farm Research Network tests products in farmers' own fields with replicated strips. In 2016 in Butler County, Vitazyme at 7, 13 and 26 oz/ac with starter on pivot-irrigated, no-till soybeans yielded 66 to 67 bu/ac, the same as the 67 bu/ac untreated check. The treated plants scored higher on a chlorophyll meter in June, but yield, oil and protein did not change, and the check earned the highest net return. A second 2016 trial applying Vitazyme at first flower on dryland soybeans gave the same result: 68 to 69 bu/ac against 68 for the check, with the check again the most profitable.

Nebraska Extension also pooled replicated trials of two soybean seed-applied biostimulants, BioForge and Optimize, across eastern Nebraska from 2009 to 2014. On rainfed fields they averaged 1.6 bu/ac more than untreated seed, 50.3 against 48.6 bu/ac. On irrigated fields the 0.9 bu/ac difference was not statistically significant. If your sandy fields are under pivots, the irrigated results are the closer match.

## What Iowa trials found

USDA-ARS researchers tested a micronized humic product in two rainfed central Iowa fields between 2012 and 2016. On an eroded hilltop, it raised corn yield 11 to 19% in the 2012 drought and 7% in dry 2013. In the wetter 2014 and 2016 seasons the gains were small or absent, and none of 15 soil properties measured responded. A wider Iowa study by the same group found gains of 1 to 4% across five replicated site-years. Humic products can help corn, but the response is modest and shows up mostly under drought stress.

Practical Farmers of Iowa ran 16 replicated farmer trials of biological products from 2019 to 2024, and 81% showed no benefit. A few results show the range:

- **Humic acid in-furrow on soybeans (2024):** 77 bu/ac against 80 for the check, a significant yield loss. Humic acid plus ammonium thiosulfate applied before planting gave 79 against 78, no difference.
- **Utrisha N on corn (2024):** a 10 bu/ac difference that was not significant, and $26.12/ac less profit after product and application cost. The 2023 Utrisha N trials also found no yield effect.
- **EnSoil Algae on corn (2024):** a 49% yield gain in one field and no significant difference in a second field on the same farm.
- **Biochar seed coating on corn (2024):** significant gains of 6 and 10 bu/ac at two farms and a non-significant 10 bu/ac at a third. At $3.52/ac, one farmer reported $22/ac more profit.

## Test a product before you buy it for every acre

Nebraska Extension notes that many biological products are not registered or regulated, so independent efficacy data can be hard to find, and field results across locations have been mixed. Ask the seller for replicated, independent results from sandy soils and from irrigated or dryland fields like yours. Then run your own test:

- Lay out at least four pairs of treated and untreated strips, randomly assigned, with the same fertilizer, hybrid and operations on both.
- If the product claims to replace nutrients, compare your full rate, a reduced rate with the product and the reduced rate alone, as Nebraska Extension recommends.
- Harvest with a calibrated yield monitor or weigh wagon and record product and application cost.
- Multiply the yield difference by your grain price and subtract the cost per acre. Repeat for a second season before scaling up.

The [Nebraska On-Farm Research Network](https://on-farm-research.unl.edu/) publishes a grower's guide and standard protocols for on-farm trials, including one for biologicals, and a results database where you can look up earlier product tests before you plan your own. Nebraska Extension suggests joining the network so a specialist can help design the study.

question: What are some specific soil health challenges that producers and agribusiness stakeholders in the Midwest region, primarily involved in corn and soybean production, might want to address through the Soil Health Exchange platform?
question_title: Which soil health problems cost Midwest corn and soybean farms the most?
expert_answer:
## Eroded hilltops are costing yield now

Thaler and colleagues used satellite images and LiDAR elevation data to map topsoil loss across the Corn Belt. They estimated that 35% (±11%) of cultivated land has lost its dark, carbon-rich A horizon, and that convex hilltops are often stripped of it completely. They linked that loss to a 6% (±2%) yield reduction, about $2.8 billion a year, and pointed to tillage moving soil downhill as an important driver. On your farm these are the light-colored knolls that stand out on a bare-soil image or yield map. Keep them covered with residue or a cover crop, cut tillage passes over them, and manage them as their own zone.

Figure 2. A-horizon loss and associated economic losses within the Corn Belt. (A) Aggregated percent A-horizon loss (black text) and annual economic losses expressed in millions of dollars (M) and as a percentage relative to uneroded soils (green text) for each state within the region (color scale is the same as in B). (B) Percentage of A-horizon loss for each county. (C) Percent annual economic losses for each county relative to predictions for uneroded soils. (D) Predicted mean annual economic losses per farm in each county. The LGM and pre-LGM glacial extent, which define the distribution of glacial till- and loess-derived soils, are shown as solid and dashed lines, respectively.Photo: Image from Thaler et al., (2021): https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1922375118

## Nutrients are leaving below ground

USDA's Conservation Effects Assessment Project compared U.S. cropland in 2003–06 with 2015–16. As no-till and other conservation practices spread, erosion, sediment and surface nitrogen losses improved. Over the same period, nitrogen lost through subsurface flow rose by 420,000 tons (13%) and soluble phosphorus losses by 7,200 tons (11%), as more water soaked into the soil and less fertilizer was worked in. Losses were concentrated: 28% of acres produced 73% of the subsurface nitrogen loss. Residue and no-till protect the surface, but on tiled ground they need to be paired with better nitrogen rate, timing and placement and with living cover that takes up nitrate after harvest.

## Compaction and wet fields hold back roots

Short planting and harvest windows push heavy equipment onto wet soil. University of Minnesota Extension reports that axle loads of 10 tons or more on wet soil can compact soil to 2 feet or deeper, below the reach of tillage, and that a single pass at 20 tons per axle in Waseca, Minnesota, still reduced corn yield 12 years later. Keeping axle loads under 10 tons confines compaction to the top 6 to 10 inches, where tillage and roots can reach it. Controlled traffic lanes, correct tire inflation and staying off wet fields when you can all limit the damage. Compaction slows infiltration and drainage and cuts air exchange in the root zone, so compacted spots are often the same spots that pond after a heavy rain.

## Where to start on your farm

Soil biology belongs on the list too. Soybean cyst nematode caused an estimated 72.6 million bushels of soybean loss across the northern states in 2024, the largest of any soybean disease, according to the Crop Protection Network. The biggest barriers to change are money and time. In the 2022–2023 national cover crop survey, 60% of the 151 farmers not using cover crops called no measurable economic return a major concern, and 51% said the same of the time and labor required.

That makes it worth targeting the practice to the problem that costs you most:

- Overlay several years of yield maps on elevation and soil maps to find eroded knolls, wet spots and compacted headlands.
- Soil sample those zones and a productive zone for organic matter, and include an SCN egg count in soybean fields.
- Pick one problem zone, change one practice there, and compare its yield and soil results with the rest of the field for at least three seasons.

question: "I farm with my dad in southwest Nebraska in Hayes County. We farm roughly 3,000 acres, all of which is dryland. We produce wheat, corn and grain sorghum. We have one field in particular that has us stumped. The field is 99 acres. Its soil type is Blackwood silt loam. We had terraces built on this field in 2010. Prior to the terraces being built, it was consistently one of our best-yielding fields. Since the terraces were built, it has become one of our worst-yielding fields. This field was also ripped shortly after the terraces were built to try to prevent any compaction issues that may have resulted from the construction of the terraces. None of the fertility programs we have tried seem to remedy the problem. Any insight into the causation of this problem, or any solutions you might be aware of would be greatly appreciated."
question_title: Why did our best dryland field yield worse after we built terraces?
expert_answer:
## What terrace construction does to a field

Level terraces hold runoff in a flat channel behind a ridge, a design suited to semi-arid areas such as southwest Nebraska with slopes up to about 4%. Building them moves a lot of soil. University of Missouri and NRCS guidance notes that topsoil is often removed during terrace construction and that areas of exposed subsoil reduce crop production. Blackwood soils formed in loess and have a neutral surface over moderately alkaline subsoil, with free carbonates (lime) starting 20 to 36 inches down. Where scrapers cut below the topsoil, the new surface is lower in organic matter, and in the deepest cuts it may be limy.

Heavy equipment also compacts soil, restricting roots and slowing infiltration. Level channels can pond water in wet spells while ridges and cut slopes stay dry, and the fertile topsoil that was moved ends up spread unevenly, so some parts of the field gained nutrients and others lost them.

## Why fertilizer programs haven't fixed it

A whole-field program averages good and poor ground. Colorado State Extension cautions that a composite sample from the entire field will not reflect conditions in eroded or leveled areas. Exposed subsoil is a common place for micronutrient shortfalls. University of Nebraska–Lincoln (UNL) guidance lists terraced or leveled land, removed topsoil and calcareous soil above pH 7.3 as conditions where zinc may be needed, and corn is sensitive to low zinc. A DTPA zinc test below 0.4 ppm is low, and 0.4 to 0.8 ppm is medium. Iron chlorosis is commonly associated with high-lime soils, and UNL rates grain sorghum as a crop likely to lose yield where it occurs.

Ripping after construction was a sound idea, but it works only under the right conditions. UNL's compaction guide says to rip when the soil is dry to tillage depth and to run the shank 1 to 2 inches below the compacted layer. Ripped soil can re-compact if it is worked wet or traffic is not controlled.

## Map the problem, then target it

- Overlay yield maps or drone or satellite imagery on the terrace layout and check whether low yields follow the cut areas, the channels or the ridges.
- Sample cut, fill, channel and undisturbed areas separately for organic matter, pH, free lime, phosphorus and zinc.
- Check for compaction with a penetrometer or bulk density samples, and dig to see where roots stop.
- Put manure on the cut areas first. In an 18-year experiment on a newly built terrace, manure alone or with fertilizer raised soil quality more than fertilizer alone, and soil quality tracked crop yield. Colorado State also reports manure is quite effective at eliminating zinc deficiency.
- Keep wheel traffic to set lanes, and stay with no-till or reduced tillage.
- Ask NRCS or an agricultural engineer to check whether channels pond and water spreads as designed.

Expect a gradual recovery. On a severely eroded hilltop in western North Dakota, North Dakota State researchers needed repeated manure applications, about 10 tons per acre a year for up to three years and then about 20 tons per acre, before soil organic matter and available nitrate rose significantly. Cover crops can add organic matter and protect against erosion, but in a dryland wheat, corn and sorghum rotation they also use water, so try them on a few acres first.

This answer was adapted from The Soil Health Exchange column in CropWatch, University of Nebraska–Lincoln. [Read the original article.](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/2023/soil-health-exchange-terrace-effects-soil-fertility-yield/)

question: Are virtual fence or collar works as they promise? what are the challenges, and is there any subscription, a farmer have to pay? Is it worthwhile and cost-effective? Have anyone use any of these :Drover, Monil, Vence, NoFence, Gallagher (eShepherd), Skygraze, Collie or Halte and share your experience?
question_title: Do virtual fence collars really work for cattle, and are the subscriptions worth paying?
expert_answer:
## Cattle learn the boundary within a week

A collar tracks each animal by GPS. As it nears the line you draw in the app, it plays an audio tone, then gives a brief electrical pulse if the animal keeps walking. University of Alberta researchers used Nofence collars to run rotational grazing for two summers. Heifers new to the system adapted in 5 to 7 days. Pulses per audio cue fell from 17.9% during training to 5.2% once rotational grazing began. A year later, the same animals as first-calf cows received pulses on 1.6% of cues during retraining and 2.2% during grazing. Cattle stayed inside the virtual boundaries more than 99% of the time.

New Mexico State University Extension recommends starting with a virtual line laid over an existing physical fence, putting the whole herd on collars at once, and moving to harder jobs such as keeping cattle out of a creek only after they have learned the basics. Plan at least six months before you start.

## What the collars cost to run

All of the major systems carry a recurring per-collar fee. University of Arizona Cooperative Extension compared companies in April 2024 using a 100-cow, 10,000-acre example:

- **Gallagher eShepherd:** collars bought at $250; $24 per collar per year on cellular, or $18 with $5,000 base stations. About $74 per cow per year over five years on cellular, $88 with two base stations.
- **Nofence:** collars bought at $329, cellular only; yearly fee of $36 to $56 per collar depending on herd size and year. About $105 per cow per year over five years, including chargers and spare batteries.
- **Vence:** collars leased at $40 per year plus two $10 batteries a year; base stations $10,000 to $12,500; 200-acre minimum. About $110 per cow per year over five years.
- **Halter:** collars leased on a two-year contract at $60 per year; base stations about $3,000. About $72 per cow per year over five years.

Prices have shifted since that comparison, so get current quotes. Herd minimums also narrow the field for a smaller herd: a Kansas State University overview from August 2026 lists Nofence at 5 or more animals, Monil at 6, eShepherd at 20, and Halter and Vence at 100. Drover uses ear tags with electrical muscle stimulation instead of collars; the company says it will not be for sale until early 2027 and has not released pricing. We found no independent trial data for Skygraze or Collie, so ask those companies for replicated results before buying.

## Coverage, collar losses and fence costs decide whether it pays

Cellular collars need a signal, and some rural areas lack the data plans they depend on. Base-station systems reach farther, but their range depends on topography, which matters in hollows and creek bottoms. Gallagher now runs eShepherd on cellular where coverage exists and keeps base stations as an option. In April 2026, Halter launched direct-to-satellite collars in the United States that need no cell or radio towers. Collars can also be knocked off by brush, rough ground or predators, and bulls lose them often. Keep your perimeter fence; virtual fencing manages your cattle inside it.

The economics are strongest where the collars replace fence you would otherwise build. New Mexico State puts new five-wire fence at about $16,000 per mile, and over $40,000 in difficult terrain. For a Kentucky hay and pasture operation, the best uses are rotating paddocks on permanent pasture, resting regrowth and keeping cattle out of streams.

We found no Kentucky or Southeast trials in tall fescue pasture. On KY-31 fescue, plan training around summer slump: University of Kentucky Extension notes that cattle on endophyte-infected fescue become heat sensitive in summer and spend more time in shade, ponds and streams instead of grazing. Spring or fall is a better time to teach a new boundary.

Next step: check phone signal across your back pastures and creek bottoms, and ask each vendor how their collars connect where it drops out. Then price the cross-fence you would otherwise build and compare it with a five-year collar cost per head for your herd size. The University of Kentucky forage extension program can tell you whether anyone nearby is running collars.

question:
I have a question. I planted wheat on October 10th, it is my first crop that I'm MANAGING. My goal is to grow it without herbicides or fungicide or synthetic fertilizer.
First off, is a traditional soil test still helpful? I know there is growing skepticism, just asking the question.
Also, recommendations for fertility/weed management would be appreciated. I'm thinking I'd opt for composted poultry litter, but am open to suggestions. My plan is to frost seed either red clover or bird's foot trefoil to fix nitrogen and also compete with weeds.
It sounds like in my area that if a guy wants to sell wheat to the mill, he best spray a fungicide. But as I said, I really don't want to do that of possible.
Any suggestions would be much appreciated! Thank you!
I'm in Pierce County, WI for reference
question_title: Growing milling wheat without herbicides, fungicides, or synthetic fertilizer in western Wisconsin
expert_answer:
Question source: Everything Cover Crops page, collected by Saurav.

You have three decisions to work through: how to feed the wheat already planted, how to keep weeds from taking over, and how to produce grain your mill can accept. The October planting date suggests winter wheat. Start by confirming the variety and the mill's requirements; those details shape the rest of the plan.

## Yes, get a standard soil test

A standard soil test remains useful when you avoid synthetic fertilizer. Ask a lab using Wisconsin interpretations for pH, lime requirement, organic matter, phosphorus, and potassium. These results help you decide whether lime or purchased nutrients are needed and whether poultry litter would add phosphorus the field already has. [UW soil-test guidance](https://cropsandsoils.extension.wisc.edu/nutrient-application-guidelines-for-field-vegetable-and-fruit-crops-in-wisconsin-a2809/soil-test-procedures/) describes the routine tests.

Use those results alongside the previous crop, manure history, and field observations. Wisconsin's wheat nitrogen recommendations follow a separate process from its phosphorus and potassium recommendations. A routine report alone does not give you the complete nitrogen budget. Tell the adviser whether you will remove straw, too; that changes nutrient removal. [UW small-grain fertility guidance](https://cropsandsoils.extension.wisc.edu/articles/soil-fertility-overview-for-small-grain-production-in-wisconsin-a-one-stop-shop/) explains these distinctions.

JoAnn Holloway of USGS and Ron Wiederholt of NDSU collect soil samples. Representative sampling is the starting point for a useful soil test.Photo: Kathleen M. Rowland, U.S. Geological Survey

## Test the litter before choosing a rate

Composted poultry litter is a possible nutrient source. Get a representative analysis for total nitrogen, ammonium nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and moisture. Ask whether the material is fully composted or simply stored litter: those materials can release nitrogen differently. Thorough composting generally slows nitrogen release, and total nitrogen on the analysis is larger than the amount available to the crop in the first season. [WSU's manure and compost guide](https://pubs.extension.wsu.edu/product/fertilizing-with-manure/) explains the difference.

Have a Wisconsin nutrient adviser estimate plant-available nitrogen for the actual material, application timing, and surface placement over your standing wheat. Count earlier manure and legume credits. Check the resulting phosphorus load against the soil test before buying enough litter to meet the entire nitrogen need. If that would oversupply phosphorus, compare a lower-phosphorus organic nitrogen source using its analysis and delivered cost. [UW manure-N guidance](https://cropsandsoils.extension.wisc.edu/articles/approaches-to-estimating-manure-nitrogen-credits/) explains availability and application losses; [UW manure guidance](https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/using-manure-in-the-home-garden/) explains the phosphorus buildup problem.

## Choose clover for the next stage of the rotation

Red clover is the better-supported first choice for frost seeding into winter wheat. Its principal nitrogen benefit comes after the clover grows, is terminated, and decomposes for the following crop. Budget this wheat crop separately. [UW's wheat and red-clover guide](https://ipcm.wisc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/54/2022/11/RedClover_0109.pdf) describes that sequence.

Broadcast inoculated seed when repeated freezing and thawing can work it into exposed soil. Good seed contact matters; deep snow or a thick residue mat can prevent an even stand. Birdsfoot trefoil establishes more slowly and is a less dependable choice for this short establishment window. Select the clover type and seeding rate with local advice and plan how to terminate it before the next crop. [Penn State's frost-seeding guide](https://extension.psu.edu/frost-seeding-a-technique-for-interseeding-cover-crops-and-improving-forage-stands) compares the species.

## Manage weeds around the stand you have

Walk the field now and again at spring green-up. Record thin patches and identify the weeds. A vigorous wheat stand does much of the weed suppression; late-planted wheat with limited tillering can leave more room for weeds. [MSU's green-up guidance](https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/winter-wheat-greenup-and-management-decisions) explains why spring stand assessment matters.

Treat clover as a partner that grows strongly after wheat harvest. Plan to remove small, troublesome weed patches before they set seed. If you have a tine weeder or rotary hoe, get advice on crop stage and test a short strip first: crop anchorage, weed size, soil conditions, and the young clover determine whether that pass is useful. For the next wheat crop, use this year's weed map to choose the preceding crop and establishment plan.

## Plan for head blight and the mill's quality limits

Ask whether the advice you heard concerns Fusarium head blight, also called head scab. It can reduce yield and contaminate wheat with DON, a mycotoxin that can lead to discounts or rejection. UW recommends flowering-time fungicide as an important tool for reducing that risk in Wisconsin. If you choose to grow without fungicide, the plan needs to account for the protection you are giving up. [UW small-grain disease guidance](https://cropsandsoils.extension.wisc.edu/articles/fungicide-use-on-small-grains-in-wisconsin/) explains the stakes.

Check the planted variety's head-blight rating and the preceding crop; corn residue is an important risk factor. For future plantings, make disease resistance and rotation part of the seed decision. Track a [head-blight risk forecast](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/crop-disease-forecasting) as the wheat approaches flowering, using its growth stage and variety susceptibility. A forecast helps anticipate risk; grain testing establishes the harvested lot's DON level.

Get the mill's acceptance specifications now, including wheat class, protein, test weight, moisture, DON, and any production requirements. Plan timely harvest and representative grain sampling. Visible scab and DON do not always match, so test the grain even when the heads look acceptable. [Wisconsin harvest guidance](https://badgercropnetwork.com/fusarium-head-blight-in-wisconsin-winter-wheat-a-guide-for-harvest-preparation/) explains this mismatch.

Your next useful step is to bring the seed label, soil report, previous-crop history, and litter analysis to a local crop adviser, and get the mill's specifications alongside them. That gives you a workable fertility plan for this wheat and a clear role for clover after harvest.

question: A Callao grower likes the corn response to Y-drop nitrogen, but the application overlaps soybean spraying, haymaking, wheat harvest and double-crop soybean planting. Could planter-applied liquid, stabilized broadcast nitrogen or a micronutrient package deliver a similar result? The grower wonders whether boron helped.
question_title: Can corn keep the Y-drop response without a sidedress pass?
expert_answer:
## Which part of the Y-drop program is paying?

Y-drops place liquid nitrogen beside the row late enough to shorten the time between application and rapid corn uptake. Surface bands still benefit from rain moving nitrogen into moist rooting soil. If you also changed the total N rate, fertilizer source, inhibitor or micronutrients, any of those changes could be behind the response. In two years of Michigan State trials, Y-drop had no overall yield advantage over injected liquid N at the same timing and rate. Little rain fell in the first week after sidedress.

## Fit the replacement to the field and planter

On well-drained fields, compare the current split with a spring preplant program you can get done on time. If you already broadcast, surface-applied urea can fit ahead of a soaking rain that moves it into the soil. A urease inhibitor can buy time before incorporation. A nitrification inhibitor slows conversion of ammonium to nitrate and addresses a different loss pathway. On soils that routinely pond or saturate, keep an option to apply some N later, including custom application if the crew is tied up.

Planter liquid can carry starter in an off-seed band, commonly 2 inches to the side and 2 inches below the seed. Before moving bulk N to the planter, work out safe placement and rate, how many acres a tank covers, and whether refill time would slow planting. Keep bulk N out of the seed furrow.

## Make one comparison you can use next year

Run replicated strips of the existing Y-drop program and one simpler program. Match total actual pounds of N per acre and other nutrients, and log fertilizer source, placement, dates and rain. Compare grain revenue minus fertilizer and application costs per acre. Count the hours each system takes during the busy week. If boron is still in question, compare with and without boron under the same N program. Missouri Extension saw one statistically significant corn response in 21 trials and no average yield benefit. Once the simpler program works, test several N rates to find the point where the next pound of N costs as much as the additional grain it produces.
